headline_speed_vs_minimap2.short_description: Headline: mean alignment latency vs. minimap2 (4 algorithms)
headline_speed_vs_minimap2.long_description: First chart by design — the headline 'how fast are we vs. minimap2?' answer. Y axis: mean per-pair alignment latency in milliseconds (lower is better, log scale). X axis: sequence length bucket (SHORT/MEDIUM/LONG/VERY_LONG). Only the two minimap2 baselines and the two bioseq KSW2 variants whose chaining matches minimap2 (scalar-DP, SIMD-DP) participate, so the visual comparison is apples-to-apples. The full 14-algorithm grid is plotted further down (`seq_length_vs_speed_mean`) for users who want every variant.

title.text: Headline: mean latency by length bucket — bioseq vs. minimap2

headline_accuracy_vs_minimap2_per_length.short_description: Headline: position accuracy vs. minimap2 (by length bucket)
headline_accuracy_vs_minimap2_per_length.long_description: Position-accuracy fraction by length bucket for the two minimap2 baselines and the two bioseq KSW2 variants. A flat line at 1.0 means the algorithm is indifferent to read length; a downward slope at the long end usually points at chaining failures or seed drop-out. Buckets the runner skipped (the `should_skip_cell` rules — see `matrix_runner.cppm`) show as missing points; lines connect across the gap.

title.text: Headline: position accuracy by length bucket

headline_accuracy_vs_minimap2_per_error.short_description: Headline: position accuracy vs. minimap2 (by error rate bucket)
headline_accuracy_vs_minimap2_per_error.long_description: Position-accuracy fraction across the six error-rate buckets, ordered HIFI -> CCS -> ONT_MODERN -> ONT_LEGACY -> HIGH_INDEL_LOW_SUB -> HIGH_SUB_LOW_INDEL. The first four buckets are calibrated against published long-read error profiles (see SOME_BENCHMARKING_PAPERS.md and the ErrorRateBucket enum in matrix_runner.cppm); the last two are exotic indel-only / sub-only stress tests inspired by the PeerJ Fig. 7 sweep. Watch for accuracy collapse at the ONT_LEGACY / HIGH_INDEL crossover — that's where minimap2's default k/w (15, 10) starts to lose seeds.

title.text: Headline: position accuracy by error rate

headline_pareto_speed_vs_accuracy.short_description: Headline: speed vs. accuracy Pareto (4 algorithms)
headline_pareto_speed_vs_accuracy.long_description: Per (algorithm, length-bucket) marker: X is mean latency in ms (lower is better), Y is position-accuracy fraction (higher is better). Points in the upper-left dominate (faster AND more accurate); points in the lower-right are dominated. The full 14-algorithm Pareto further down (`pareto_accuracy_vs_latency`) preserves every variant.

kmer_window_accuracy_minimap2.long_description: Accuracy fraction for the C minimap2 reference as (k, w) vary over the canonical preset combinations: k in {10, 15, 19, 21, 25}, w in {5, 10, 11}. Run on the MEDIUM/CCS bucket (5 kbp pairs at ~1.5% error) so that every cell completes in seconds and the signal isolates the parameter impact. Brighter (higher) cells = better accuracy. Sweep cells with zero samples render as missing (Plotly null); see `run_kw_sweep` in matrix_runner.cppm for which (k, w) combinations are exercised.

kmer_window_accuracy_bioseq.short_description: k/w sweep — accuracy heatmap (bioseq KSW2 + scalar-DP + scalar-mm)
kmer_window_accuracy_bioseq.long_description: Same axes as the minimap2 k/w heatmap, restricted to the bioseq KSW2 + scalar-DP + scalar-mm variant (the closest algorithmic match to minimap2's default chain+align pipeline). Direct compare: a cell that's brighter here than in the minimap2 heatmap means our port is more sensitive at that (k, w) point; darker = less sensitive. Use to spot (k, w) regions where the port has a bug or has gained an advantage.

title.text: k/w sweep — accuracy heatmap (bioseq KSW2 + scalar-DP + scalar-mm)

kmer_window_speed_minimap2.short_description: k/w sweep — mean latency heatmap (minimap2 reference)
kmer_window_speed_minimap2.long_description: Mean per-pair latency (ms) for the C minimap2 reference as (k, w) vary. Cividis colourmap — darker = faster. Smaller k produces more minimizers (denser hit table, slower seeding); smaller w produces more minimizers per window (denser still). Read together with the accuracy heatmap to pick the (k, w) point with the best sensitivity / speed trade-off.

title.text: k/w sweep — mean latency heatmap (minimap2 reference)

kmer_window_speed_bioseq.short_description: k/w sweep — mean latency heatmap (bioseq KSW2 + scalar-DP + scalar-mm)
kmer_window_speed_bioseq.long_description: Same axes as the minimap2 k/w speed heatmap, restricted to the bioseq KSW2 + scalar-DP + scalar-mm variant. Compare to the minimap2 version above: cells where bioseq is darker (faster) indicate the port has a real speed advantage at that (k, w); cells where bioseq is lighter (slower) are the candidates for further optimization work.

title.text: k/w sweep — mean latency heatmap (bioseq KSW2 + scalar-DP + scalar-mm)

seq_length_vs_speed_mean.short_description: Mean alignment latency vs. effective query length
seq_length_vs_speed_mean.long_description: Mean wall-clock latency per (query, target) pair as a function of the effective query length (post-error length, in bp). One trace per algorithm configuration; both axes log-scale because the length axis spans short reads (300 bp) through assembly fragments (2 Mbp). Lower lines = faster algorithms. Use this chart to spot algorithmic complexity: linear-in-length lines indicate O(n) behaviour, super-linear curves point at O(n log n) or worse regions in the chosen pipeline.

title.text: Mean alignment latency vs. effective query length

seq_length_vs_speed_p99.short_description: Pooled P50 and P99 latency per (algorithm, length bucket)
seq_length_vs_speed_p99.long_description: Per-bucket pooled P50 and P99 latencies. For each algorithm and length bucket we pool every per-sample timing across all pairs in that bucket (16 pairs × 8 samples = 128 samples for SHORT, 24 for MEDIUM, 12 for LONG, 1 for VERY_LONG) before computing percentiles, so the P99 is over a sufficient sample size (except VERY_LONG, where it degenerates to the single observation). Solid markers = P50, hollow markers = P99. The vertical gap between the two for one algorithm is the tail width: large gaps indicate a heavy-tailed latency distribution and small gaps indicate a tight distribution.

title.text: P50 (solid) and P99 (dashed open) per length bucket — pooled

seq_length_vs_memory.short_description: Working-set delta (current RSS) vs. effective query length
seq_length_vs_memory.long_description: Mean increase in current resident-set size per aligner invocation, plotted against the effective query length. The RSS reading uses `task_info(TASK_BASIC_INFO).resident_size` on macOS and `/proc/self/statm` on Linux — instantaneous current-RSS, not lifetime peak — so the per-call delta is a live working-set measurement. Negative deltas (the allocator released pages between calls) are clamped to zero so the y axis stays positive. Traces with all-zero deltas are hidden.

title.text: Mean RSS delta vs. effective query length

seq_length_vs_accuracy.short_description: Position accuracy vs. sequence length bucket
seq_length_vs_accuracy.long_description: Fraction of (query, target) pairs whose primary alignment lands within tolerance of the simulated truth, bucketed by sequence length. Every algorithm trace spans all four length buckets — buckets with no samples (e.g. RMQ + VERY_LONG when skipped) are emitted as JSON null so the line connects the remaining points without misrepresenting missing data as zero. A flat line near 1.0 means the algorithm is indifferent to read length; a downward slope at the long / very-long end usually points at chaining failures or seed drop-out. The minimap2 reference traces are the de-facto upper bound — bioseq variants below them indicate a regression in the corresponding phase.

title.text: Position accuracy vs. sequence length bucket

error_rate_vs_accuracy.short_description: Position accuracy vs. simulated error rate
error_rate_vs_accuracy.long_description: Grouped bar chart of position accuracy across the three error buckets (low / medium / high). Each bar group corresponds to one error rate; bars within a group are the algorithm configurations. Use this chart to identify configurations that degrade gracefully (their bar shrinks slowly across buckets) vs. those that collapse beyond the medium bucket. The error rate is the sum of substitution + insertion + deletion rates applied to each fragment by the SEAL-style generator.

title.text: Position accuracy vs. simulated error rate

accuracy_heatmap_algorithm_vs_length.long_description: Heatmap whose rows are algorithm configurations and columns are length buckets; cell colour encodes the fraction of correctly-placed primaries. White / yellow cells highlight (algorithm, length) combinations that need attention. The heatmap collapses the full per-pair detail into a single grid so reviewer attention can be drawn to outlier cells before drilling into per-pair charts.

title.text: Position accuracy by algorithm and length bucket

latency_distribution_box.long_description: Box-and-whisker plot per (algorithm, length-bucket) cell. The box renders the 25th-75th percentile range, the whiskers extend to 1.5× IQR (Plotly default), and the median is the horizontal line inside the box. Outliers are drawn as individual points. Tall whiskers / many outlier dots indicate an algorithm with high tail-latency variance for that length class. Compare to Chart 1 (mean) and Chart 2 (P99) to triangulate where the P99 - mean gap comes from.

seq_length_vs_throughput.long_description: Aligner throughput, in megabases-per-second, derived as effective_query_length / mean_latency. Throughput-normalised view of Chart 1: a flat horizontal trace means the algorithm's per-base cost is constant across length classes; a sloping trace means the per-base cost changes (e.g. cache effects on long reads, or super-linear chaining). Use this view when comparing pipelines whose absolute latency differs by orders of magnitude — the units cancel out the length dependence.

p99_over_mean_tail_amplification.short_description: Tail-amplification (P99 / mean) by algorithm and length bucket
p99_over_mean_tail_amplification.long_description: P99 / mean ratio per algorithm and length bucket. Values close to 1 indicate tight latency distributions; values above 3-5 flag aligners that are dominated by a small fraction of slow inputs (relevant when sizing latency budgets for interactive workloads). The chart is rendered as one trace per algorithm with the length bucket on the x-axis.

position_offset_histogram.long_description: Distribution of signed position offsets (aligner_start - truth_start, in bp) across every benchmark sample, broken down by algorithm. A sharp spike at 0 with thin tails = the aligner places primaries on or next to the simulated truth. Wide skirts = drift; bimodal distributions = the aligner frequently locks onto an alternate repeat. Bins are clipped to ±100 bp; offsets beyond that fold into the edge bins.

speedup_vs_minimap2_reference_dp.short_description: Paired speedup vs. minimap2 (DP chaining) per length bucket
speedup_vs_minimap2_reference_dp.long_description: Per-bucket paired speedup ratio vs. the minimap2 (DP) baseline. For each (length_bucket, error_bucket) cell we compute the cell's mean of `mm2_DP_mean_ns / variant_mean_ns` (equivalently: per-pair speedup, averaged over pairs). Bars above 1 = bioseq faster than minimap2; bars below 1 = slower. Pairing makes the comparison robust to one slow outlier dominating either operand. The two minimap2 traces are excluded (DP would always be at 1.0 by construction; RMQ is a different reference).

title.text: Paired speedup ratio vs. minimap2 (DP chaining)

mapq_distribution.long_description: Histogram of primary mapping qualities (MAPQ, 0-60) per algorithm. Aligners that bin most primaries at MAPQ=60 (or near it) have high confidence in their placements; aligners with mass spread across the lower buckets are uncertain about where reads belong (often the right call when the input is ambiguous). MAPQ is a Phred-scaled score — 60 corresponds to 1-in-1,000,000 expected misplacement.

latency_cdf_per_algorithm.short_description: Empirical CDF of per-sample latency per algorithm
latency_cdf_per_algorithm.long_description: Empirical cumulative distribution function of per-sample latency, with all samples pooled across length buckets and error rates. X axis is the sorted latency in ms (log scale); Y axis is the cumulative probability. Read horizontally to find any percentile (P50 = where the trace crosses Y=0.5, P99 at Y=0.99, etc.). Two traces crossing means one algorithm wins at low percentiles but the other wins at the tail — common pattern when one variant has lower mean but longer tail. Strictly more informative than the single-number P99 charts.

pareto_accuracy_vs_latency.short_description: Pareto frontier — accuracy vs. mean latency
pareto_accuracy_vs_latency.long_description: Per (algorithm, length-bucket) marker: X is mean latency in ms (lower is better), Y is position-accuracy fraction (higher is better). The 'Pareto frontier' is the set of points where no other configuration is strictly better in both dimensions — those are the live trade-offs. Configurations strictly dominated by another (worse on both axes) are bad choices regardless of the operator's accuracy/latency preference. Marker symbol encodes the length bucket so the reader can visually group by input class.

accuracy_heatmap_algorithm_vs_length_err.long_description: Heatmap rows are algorithm configurations; columns are the (length-bucket, error-rate) cells in the sweep matrix. Cell colour encodes the position-accuracy fraction in that cell. Unlike the algorithm × length-only heatmap, this view preserves the error-rate axis — a configuration that's perfect on HIFI-error but collapses on ONT_LEGACY-error appears as two distinct columns rather than averaging to 50%. Cells the runner skipped (ONT_LEGACY/HIGH_INDEL × LONG, RMQ × VERY_LONG, etc.) show up as 0 — hover for the per-cell sample count to disambiguate.

title.text: Position accuracy by algorithm and (length, error) cell

mapq_calibration.short_description: MAPQ calibration curve (accuracy by MAPQ bin)
mapq_calibration.long_description: For each algorithm we bin primaries into 10-wide MAPQ bins (0-9, 10-19, ..., 50-60) and report the fraction correctly placed in each bin. A well-calibrated aligner produces a monotonic curve climbing from low accuracy at low MAPQ to ~1.0 at MAPQ=60 (since MAPQ is Phred-scaled and 60 means 1-in-1,000,000 expected misplacement). Curves that cluster at high accuracy across all MAPQs indicate MAPQ deflation (the aligner is more confident than its scores reflect); curves with low accuracy at high MAPQ indicate inflation.

title.text: MAPQ calibration — accuracy by MAPQ bin

phase_breakdown_short.short_description: Per-pipeline-phase mean ns per timed sample, stacked, for every bioseq config in the short (<1kb) length bucket
phase_breakdown_short.long_description: Stacked bar chart with one X-axis category per bioseq algorithm config (minimap2 reference rows omitted — their instrumentation aggregates are not attributed by phase). Each stack segment is a pipeline phase (mm_sketch, target_index_build, collect_seed_hits, mg_lchain_*, mm_align_skeleton, ... — taken from the `register_region_static` literals in the source) and its height is the mean ns per timed sample for that phase, averaged across every pair in the short (<1kb) length bucket. Total bar height ≈ end-to-end mean latency for that config. Use this chart first when investigating 'why is bioseq slow on short (<1kb)-length inputs?': the dominant segment is the bottleneck. Short sequences (<1kb) — the alignment phase tends to be negligible here; bottlenecks usually surface in seed-hit collection and chaining setup.

title.text: mean wall-clock ms per sample (stacked by phase)

phase_breakdown_medium.short_description: Per-pipeline-phase mean ns per timed sample, stacked, for every bioseq config in the medium (1k-10k) length bucket
phase_breakdown_medium.long_description: Stacked bar chart with one X-axis category per bioseq algorithm config (minimap2 reference rows omitted — their instrumentation aggregates are not attributed by phase). Each stack segment is a pipeline phase (mm_sketch, target_index_build, collect_seed_hits, mg_lchain_*, mm_align_skeleton, ... — taken from the `register_region_static` literals in the source) and its height is the mean ns per timed sample for that phase, averaged across every pair in the medium (1k-10k) length bucket. Total bar height ≈ end-to-end mean latency for that config. Use this chart first when investigating 'why is bioseq slow on medium (1k-10k)-length inputs?': the dominant segment is the bottleneck. Medium sequences (1k-10k) — the working point most long-read benchmarks publish in. Sketching and chaining should dominate; if `mm_align_skeleton` is the tallest segment, the base aligner is a candidate for tuning.

title.text: mean wall-clock ms per sample (stacked by phase)

phase_breakdown_long.short_description: Per-pipeline-phase mean ns per timed sample, stacked, for every bioseq config in the long (10k-1M) length bucket
phase_breakdown_long.long_description: Stacked bar chart with one X-axis category per bioseq algorithm config (minimap2 reference rows omitted — their instrumentation aggregates are not attributed by phase). Each stack segment is a pipeline phase (mm_sketch, target_index_build, collect_seed_hits, mg_lchain_*, mm_align_skeleton, ... — taken from the `register_region_static` literals in the source) and its height is the mean ns per timed sample for that phase, averaged across every pair in the long (10k-1M) length bucket. Total bar height ≈ end-to-end mean latency for that config. Use this chart first when investigating 'why is bioseq slow on long (10k-1M)-length inputs?': the dominant segment is the bottleneck. Long sequences (10k-1M) — `mm_align_skeleton` typically moves into the dominant slot. Compare KSW2 vs Block aligner stacks to see whether the align phase or the chaining phase explains the gap to minimap2.

title.text: mean wall-clock ms per sample (stacked by phase)

phase_breakdown_very_long.short_description: Per-pipeline-phase mean ns per timed sample, stacked, for every bioseq config in the very long (1M-3M) length bucket
phase_breakdown_very_long.long_description: Stacked bar chart with one X-axis category per bioseq algorithm config (minimap2 reference rows omitted — their instrumentation aggregates are not attributed by phase). Each stack segment is a pipeline phase (mm_sketch, target_index_build, collect_seed_hits, mg_lchain_*, mm_align_skeleton, ... — taken from the `register_region_static` literals in the source) and its height is the mean ns per timed sample for that phase, averaged across every pair in the very long (1M-3M) length bucket. Total bar height ≈ end-to-end mean latency for that config. Use this chart first when investigating 'why is bioseq slow on very long (1M-3M)-length inputs?': the dominant segment is the bottleneck. Very long sequences (1M-3M) — for assembly-to-assembly pairs. Even the cheapest phase blows up here; the stacked breakdown reveals whether the slowdown is the alignment, the chain DP, or the per-sketch hashing amortising poorly across millions of bases.

title.text: Pipeline phase breakdown — very long (1M-3M) sequences
mean wall-clock ms per sample (stacked by phase)

headline_largest_per_stage_time.short_description: Headline: per-stage wall-clock comparison, fastest bioseq vs minimap2 on largest sequences
headline_largest_per_stage_time.long_description: Two grouped bars per logical stage (Minimizer generation, Chaining, Alignment, ...) — left bar is minimap2 (DP chaining), right bar is the fastest bioseq config (lowest summed wall-clock across stages). Y is mean wall-clock ms per call on the largest sequence bucket the bench ran. Use this chart to spot which stage is dragging bioseq behind minimap2 (or where bioseq has already overtaken).

data.name: fastest bioseq: bioseq Block + SIMD-DP + two-stack-nthash-mm

title.text: Per-stage wall-clock — fastest bioseq vs minimap2 (xl (5M-15M) bucket)

headline_largest_per_stage_cycles.short_description: Per-stage CPU cycles (every algorithm) — largest sequences
headline_largest_per_stage_cycles.long_description: Grouped bar chart: one bar per algorithm per logical stage, Y is mean PMU 'cycles' counter delta per call. Zero bars on every algo indicate the host has no PMU access (macOS without root, Linux with perf_event_paranoid > 1). Compare the bar heights side by side to see which algorithm is paying more CPU cycles for the same logical stage.

title.text: Per-stage mean CPU cycles / call (xl (5M-15M) bucket)

headline_largest_per_stage_instructions.short_description: Per-stage retired instructions (every algorithm) — largest sequences
headline_largest_per_stage_instructions.long_description: Same shape as the cycles chart but Y is mean retired-instruction counter per call. Useful complement to cycles for IPC analysis: instructions / cycles ≈ IPC.

headline_largest_per_stage_branches.short_description: Per-stage retired branches (every algorithm) — largest sequences
headline_largest_per_stage_branches.long_description: Same shape as the cycles chart but Y is mean branch-instruction counter per call. Read this beside the branch-misses chart to compute branch miss rate per stage.

headline_largest_per_stage_branch_misses.short_description: Per-stage branch mispredictions (every algorithm) — largest sequences
headline_largest_per_stage_branch_misses.long_description: Same shape as the cycles chart but Y is mean branch-mispredict counter per call. The bigger the bar, the more the stage is hurt by branch prediction noise. SIMD code with horizontal mask reductions (e.g. the slow legacy SIMD-mm) typically shows up as taller bars than its scalar peers — the production two-stack-nthash path mostly avoids this by using a uniform per-w rebuild instead of a data-dependent rescan.

title.text: Per-stage mean branch mispredicts / call (xl (5M-15M) bucket)

headline_largest_per_stage_branch_miss_r.short_description: Per-stage branch miss rate (every algorithm) — largest sequences
headline_largest_per_stage_branch_miss_r.long_description: Branch-miss rate = mispredicts / branches per stage and algorithm. Normalises out the per-stage call count so two algorithms running the same number of calls can be compared on prediction quality. A 5% miss rate on chaining is bad; a 1% miss rate on minimizer generation is normal.

headline_largest_stage_table.short_description: Headline: stage × algorithm comparison table (largest sequences, color-coded green→red)
headline_largest_stage_table.long_description: Each row is a logical pipeline stage; each column is one algorithm. Cells contain the dominant phase name + the mean wall-clock per call (e.g. 'mm_sketch_simd: 13.45 ms'). Cell background colour is a per-row gradient — green for the fastest algorithm in that stage, red for the slowest, yellow in the middle. Rows where every algorithm reports zero are coloured grey. Use this table to spot which stages bioseq dominates and which still trail minimap2.

algorithm_summary_table.long_description: Tabular roll-up of every algorithm's pair count, mean / median / P99 latency in milliseconds, and overall position-accuracy fraction. Useful as a one-glance sanity check before diving into the per-chart detail; the row ordering matches the chart legend order so the reader can cross-reference.
